title: Jeremy Doku’s late goal at Everton could mean everything in the title race. Or it could mean nothing
content:
Football is a wonderful thing, isn’t it? It may not feel like that for those of a Manchester City persuasion this morning but truth be told, could any of them sum up exactly how they feel after a thrilling, potentially disastrous 3-3 draw at Everton on Monday night?

The bare facts are obvious: City have slipped up and the title is no longer in their hands. This could easily be the night where their hopes of adding another Premier League trophy to the cabinet died.

And yet the peculiar emotions of football do not allow for things to be so black and white. This is the beauty of football: just when you think you have seen everything, something else comes along to get your head around. It has you doing and saying things that you would never do in normal circumstances, and sometimes it just downright confounds you.

There is not a City fan in the world who would have taken a point against Everton before kick-off, nor indeed an Arsenal fan on the planet who would not have snapped your hand off for their rivals dropping two, and yet the draw will not feel quite as bitter for City nor as sweet for Arsenal.

City were 1-0 up at half-time, coasting towards victory. Many fans will have started pondering their side’s goal difference. Yet with nine minutes to go, they were 3-1 down, looking completely lost. Even so, Erling Haaland struck back immediately from kick-off after Everton’s third goal and after a late rally, with goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma going up for two stoppage-time corners, Jeremy Doku curled the ball into the far corner for a 97th-minute leveller that could mean everything. Or it could mean nothing.

David Moyes, the Everton manager who helped inspire his team to their rousing second-half performance, was completely deflated in his post-match media interactions.

He said that, during the first half, his players had put in their worst big-game showing of his second spell at the club, lamenting how they had been “pushed around”, and he praised Doku’s goal as “brilliant” and “incredible”. “We have to give him credit for that,” he shrugged.

Doku was a threat throughout, illustrated in his player dashboard above

The City fans in the away end had gone crazy. Donnarumma, who stepped out of the way to make room for Doku to line up his shot, clawed at the Belgian as he peeled away in celebration, pressing his finger to his lips. It was pandemonium.

Moments later, the final whistle was blown and the City players made their way off the pitch. Bernardo Silva looked like he had seen a ghost as he trudged down the tunnel. None of them looked like they had salvaged anything as they left the stadium an hour later.

The City fans who had grabbed each other in ecstasy had to make their way home reflecting on a night when things, quite probably, went badly wrong.

Give it a couple of weeks, maybe even six days, and that late Doku goal could be one of the biggest of the season. It feels improbable, and it would require West Ham United avoiding defeat against Arsenal next Sunday, or Burnley or Crystal Palace after that, but if this season’s title race has been characterised by one thing, it is that Arsenal have always slipped up enough for this imperfect City team’s bad results to never be fully punished. In January, City took six points from a possible 15 — and yet they gained a point on Arsenal.

City have a fair few examples of moments in title races that have turned out to be truly difference-making. Think of Sergio Aguero’s goal at Burnley in 2019, which crossed the line by 29 millimetres at a time when they simply had to win every match, or Stefan Ortega’s save from Son Heung-min in 2024, four days before the final day.

Maybe the best parallel for Doku’s goal is with Vladimir Coufal’s own goal at West Ham on the penultimate weekend of the 2021-22 season. City had been 2-0 down at the break, the title looking all but gone, after weeks of battling with Liverpool, just like they had done three years earlier. Jack Grealish scored soon after half-time to offer some hope before Coufal turned into his own net to level things up and set up a late onslaught, but Riyad Mahrez missed a penalty with four minutes to go. Had they been brilliant to rescue a point or had they ruined it?

For the next seven days, it was impossible to know what it all meant, just that City had to beat Aston Villa on the final day. They did, of course, but only after falling two goals down and hitting back with three in six minutes.

Mahrez’s missed penalty could have been what his time at City became known for, but many would struggle to even remember it now because of how things panned out later.

City will be hoping that Doku’s goal goes the other way and is given the kind of importance that the quality of the finish itself deserves.

But for that, they need to beat Brentford on Saturday — not a given if they play like they did on Monday — and then get the ultimate favour from one of Arsenal’s final three opponents. It all feels unlikely, but we have seen enough football to know how narratives can change quickly. What if Arsenal go out of the Champions League? What if City put six past Brentford?

This is what football does to us. No matter how many title races we have lived through, how many times we think we know how things will pan out, nobody can ever be sure, no matter how confidently they tell you.

City fans who have lived through several unbearable title races with Liverpool, which might be looked back fondly upon now but were gruelling at the time, will know that anything can happen at this time of year.

Doku’s late strike could yet rank alongside some of the all-time moments in the club’s history.

Or it could have been for nothing. We will just have to spend the week thinking about it.
